files.compose.header:
Written by looptrack setup ({time}). A template based on deploy/compose.yaml.

  docker compose up -d           start (builds the image from the Dockerfile next to it when there is none)
  docker compose up -d --build   rebuild after replacing the executable
  docker compose logs -f         logs

- Published on 127.0.0.1:{port} only. From outside, have a reverse proxy (Nginx or the like) receive {url}/ and pass it on (without stripping the prefix).
- The settings are in .env (600, kept out of git).
files.compose.image:
The image is built from the Dockerfile in this directory (it only puts looptrack on scratch).
With build here, an image of the same name is never pulled from outside.
files.compose.sqlite:
The SQLite file lives in ./data (the container runs as uid 65534, so make it writable.
  im.db is created for its owner alone (600), so hand over the files inside too: sudo chown -R 65534:65534 data)
files.compose.mysql: When MySQL runs in a container, put this on the same Docker network (for example, add networks: [mysql] and a networks section below)
files.compose.mem_limit:
Large enough for the server (GOMEMLIMIT 64MiB) plus the second looptrack that healthcheck starts.
The scratch image has no shell and no curl, so the only health check is to run another copy of itself.
At 96m, 112m or 128m the second one hits the cgroup limit and is SIGKILLed, and even with /healthz at 200
the container stays unhealthy and keeps restarting (measured 2026-09-20).

kitinit.guide.codex:
Codex setup:

  - The AI works mainly through the MCP tools (see AGENTS.md). You add the MCP connection to ~/.codex/config.toml yourself (init does not write it):

      [mcp_servers.looptrack]
      url = "{url}/mcp"
      http_headers = { "X-Looptrack-Project" = "{slug}" }
      # Authentication is the browser approval (codex mcp login looptrack)

  - init wrote LOOPTRACK_API_URL / LOOPTRACK_PROJECT into the set of [shell_environment_policy] in .codex/config.toml (the project one)
    (for the looptrack issue commands the AI runs for what MCP does not have. It does not open the sandbox network; every CLI run still needs your approval)
  - Trusting hooks: Codex only runs hooks when the project is trusted and each hook has been trusted (untrusted or changed hooks are skipped silently). Start the Codex CLI (codex) in this directory and use /hooks to review and trust the hooks in .codex/hooks.json. The trust is recorded under [hooks.state] in ~/.codex/config.toml and applies to the desktop app too (/hooks is not a command in the desktop chat box). It takes effect in sessions started after that.
  - When init changes the hook wiring (a re-run shows "updated .codex/hooks.json"), trust the changed hooks again the same way
  - The old notify setting has been replaced by hooks (existing notify settings are left alone; update an old Codex that has no hooks)
  - The freshness guard (which stops on Stop) is wired for Claude Code only
kitinit.guide.copilot:
GitHub Copilot setup (VS Code agent mode and Copilot CLI. Copilot CLI was checked against 1.0.86 on 2026-09-19; VS Code only against the official docs, not against the real thing):

  - The AI works mainly through the MCP tools (see AGENTS.md). You add the MCP connection yourself (init writes .vscode/mcp.json only with --mcp):
      VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json; the first connection asks for approval in the browser):
        {"servers": {"looptrack": {"type": "http", "url": "{url}/mcp", "headers": {"X-Looptrack-Project": "{slug}"}}}}
      Copilot CLI (.github/mcp.json or .mcp.json in the repository, or ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json. tools is required.
      Since 1.0.22 it no longer reads .vscode/mcp.json. init writes .github/mcp.json only with --mcp. Authentication is /mcp auth looptrack in copilot):
        {"mcpServers": {"looptrack": {"type": "http", "url": "{url}/mcp", "headers": {"X-Looptrack-Project": "{slug}"}, "tools": ["*"]}}}
    Every MCP tool call in Copilot CLI needs approval. To allow them up front, start it with copilot --allow-tool='looptrack'
  - Hooks ({hooks}): VS Code reads .github/hooks/*.json by default (a Preview feature; your organization may have it disabled).
    Copilot CLI reads them only when you trusted this folder at startup ("always trust"). Both take effect in a new session.
    The output is written in both the CLI form (top level) and the VS Code form (hookSpecificOutput). VS Code ignores matcher, so the hook itself filters on the tool name
  - Windows: the hook is looptrack (the same looptrack hook is also placed in the powershell / windows fields for PowerShell; not checked on real Windows).
    If the install is not recognized, report it with looptrack issue installed --agent copilot
  - The token metering hook (looptrack hook usage --agent copilot; PostToolUse, Stop, SessionEnd) was installed. Metering happens once you enable Copilot's OpenTelemetry file output
    (write it under ${COPILOT_HOME:-~/.copilot}/otel/. Copilot CLI does not pass the output path to the hook. See docs/AI-GUIDE.md section 7-3-1). Without it nothing is sent, and Copilot's actions are not counted as missing
  - The freshness guard (which stops on Stop) is wired for Claude Code only
  - The CLI the AI runs does not get LOOPTRACK_API_URL / LOOPTRACK_PROJECT (Copilot has no environment variable setting). AGENTS.md explains prefixing them.
kitinit.guide.other:
Setting up another coding AI (apart from placing the CLI, init writes no files. Put the following into that AI's instruction file and settings):

  1. {cli_line}
  2. Environment variables: LOOPTRACK_API_URL={url} LOOPTRACK_PROJECT={slug} (set so that they reach the shell the AI runs)
  3. Write in the instruction file (the one that AI reads every time):
     - Read `{cli} guide` at the start of the work (or the guide tool over MCP)
     - The loop: next -> work -> comment -> verify the acceptance criteria -> close --comment -> next
  4. MCP: {url}/mcp (header X-Looptrack-Project: {slug}, OAuth for authentication)
  5. If it has hooks, call looptrack hook usage after a tool run, at the end of a turn and at the end of a session (token metering; docs/server/DESIGN.md section 5-4)
  6. When the setup is done, tell the server with `{cli} installed --agent other` (the install instructions disappear from the MCP tool results)

loop.handoff.cli.usage:
Usage:
  looptrack handoff append [--title <heading>] [--file <path>] [--session <ID>] [<body> | -]
  looptrack handoff compact --sha <SHA-256 as of when you read it> [--drop-marks] [--lock-ttl <seconds>] [--file <path>] [<body> | -]

append adds a section at the end (with O_APPEND, concurrent writes from other sessions neither interleave nor get lost).
It puts the session's mark on the line right after the heading (the mark the freshness guard reads to tell who wrote it).
compact is only for rewriting the whole file. If the SHA-256 as of when you read it differs from the file, it writes nothing and refuses.
--drop-marks removes only the session mark lines (for when the parallel sessions are gone and one session is left).
The body comes from the argument, or from standard input with no argument or with -.

{list}

It shows up neither in the subagent list nor in the worktree list. Left alone, it keeps showing as "running" on the user's screen only.

What to do:
  1. Kill it if it is no longer needed

  3. Wait on CI by an identifier that cannot disappear, such as the PR number (not a SHA that a force-push removes)

loop.subagentbound.note: {mark} Do not write a loop that waits in the background. If you must wait, always carry a maximum number of attempts or a deadline, and when it is exceeded, give up and report why. Before you start waiting, confirm on the spot that the thing you are waiting on exists (if it does not, do not wait - report it then and there). Stop every background process you started yourself, and put one line in your report naming the background processes you started and that they were stopped. The scratchpad is shared by the parent and every subagent, so give every file you use for measurement a name that cannot collide (a suffix unique to your agent), and when a result comes back empty or unexpected, suspect that the measurement itself broke before you believe it.

loop.subagentmodel.deny:
[Subagent selection] This subagent launch does not specify a model.

The rules (the "Subagents" section of working-discipline.md) call for switching the model to match how hard the task is, but words alone do not make that happen (what actually happened: an inventory job that was nothing but a summary ran on the same heavy model as the parent, with no model specified). The axis is whether a mistake would be noticed.

Pick one to match the difficulty, and call it again with model set:
  1. haiku (light): work a check can mechanically reject - searching, transcribing a listing, running tests and transcribing the results, filing issues, document formatting, updating records, mechanical merges.
  2. sonnet (medium): implementation, research and summaries whose procedure is settled - the kind where a mistake turns a test or a check red.
  3. opus (heavy): work that quietly gets worse without ever failing - translation quality, consistency with how things are already written, isolating a cause, deciding what to drop, design.

It goes through once you add model and call it again. This check does not apply when subagent_type is fork (the model follows the parent), or when that type's definition file (.claude/agents/<name>.md) already carries model: in its frontmatter.

If you really need to opt out, check with the user and add the name to {env} (whitespace-separated subagent_type names; * exempts all).

Blocked an edit inside the project: this session is in review mode (task-mode contract).

The user asked you to review (investigate, report, plan), not to edit.

- The user decides when editing starts (an instruction to implement or carry it out in a later turn switches to execute mode automatically; the phrases are matched by LOOPTRACK_LOOP_TASK_MODE_EXEC_RE)
- Only when the user asks for an edit (for example in an answer to a question tool), quote that instruction and run
  echo execute > {marker}
  to switch (never switch on your own judgement)

loop.waitloop.deny:
[Background process discipline] A wait loop with no bound was stopped ({cmd}).

If what you wait on disappears along the way, or never existed, this shape can never finish (measured: two unbounded polling loops ran for over 15 hours and hit an external API roughly 6,400 times. On another day three were created in a single day, and one of them waited on a path that did not exist).

It goes through once it carries a bound. How to rewrite it:
  1. A maximum number of attempts: for i in $(seq 1 60); do <condition> && break; sleep 10; done
  2. A deadline: deadline=$((SECONDS+600)); until <condition>; do [ $SECONDS -ge $deadline ] && break; sleep 5; done
  3. Cut the whole thing off: timeout 600 <command>
When the bound is reached, do not spin on in silence - give up and report why. Before you start waiting, confirm on the spot that the thing you are waiting on exists.

If you really need the unbounded shape, check with the user and add the word to LOOPTRACK_LOOP_WAITLOOP_ALLOW (see the background-process.md rule).
loop.waitloop.missing_dir:
[Background process discipline] The parent directory {dir} of what you are waiting on ({path}) does not exist (this wait was not stopped; it does carry a bound).

Waiting for a file that does not exist yet is the right way to wait on a completion marker, but when the place it would live is missing too, the file may never be created there (the path may be wrong). Measured: of the three loops found on 2026-09-20, one waited on a path that never existed, so its exit condition could never be met.

Before you start waiting, confirm that what you wait on really is created at that path.

server.mcp.tool.assign_issue: Change the assignee (me for yourself, a login, - to clear). Changing or clearing the assignee of an issue assigned to someone else takes override_reason (taking it over; only when the user has explicitly told you to). An issue assigned to someone else cannot be moved to In Progress, nor its body edited
server.mcp.tool.create_issue: Create an issue (the server assigns the ID)
server.mcp.tool.create_project: Create a project (server administrators only). You join it as admin and can create issues in it right away. The prefix (of the IDs) and the width (digits of the number) can never be changed afterwards, so before calling this, show the user the slug, prefix and width (and the defaults, for any you leave out) and get their approval. The values follow the same rules as looptrack project create. A slug or prefix that is already taken is rejected
server.mcp.tool.get_issue: The full text of an issue (Markdown), with its version and comments
server.mcp.tool.get_matrix: The traceability table from requirements to design / implementation / test, with warnings (requirements with no test, traces pointing at issues that do not exist, requirements still open although everything below them is finished)
server.mcp.tool.guide: Returns how to use it and the rules in one go (the common rules + this project's rules + its operating document). Call it once at the start of your work
server.mcp.tool.issue_activity: The last update event per issue and the number of updates since since (to check whether you updated the issues you referred to)
server.mcp.tool.issue_usage: Tokens spent on an issue (the spans per stage and the total; the same as looptrack issue usage show). Spans from conversations excluded from reports are listed but not counted in the total
server.mcp.tool.list_issues: List issues (open ones in priority order by default; the same filters and sort orders as looptrack issue list)
server.mcp.tool.list_projects: The projects you are a member of, with counts (open, in progress, ready, open bugs). Administrators also see only the projects they belong to (a project you are not a member of can be viewed by passing its slug in project; writing to it takes membership)
server.mcp.tool.list_usage_ledger: The ledger of token reports (the period, the data end and the excluded conversations of each report made). Newest data end first
server.mcp.tool.list_usage_requests: Token report requests registered from the Create report screen (only unfinished ones by default). To answer one, total up with usage_report given request_id, and once the report is made, register it with add_usage_ledger carrying the same request_id (registering it finishes the request)
server.mcp.tool.next: Start work in the loop. If you have an issue in progress (In Progress; containers such as an epic with open children, and types outside types, are skipped), that one; otherwise the highest-ranked issue that can be started (Todo, blocked_by resolved, no open children, not an epic) is moved to In Progress. Returns its body, acceptance criteria and related issues (parent / blocked_by / traces / children). dry_run checks without changing the status
server.mcp.tool.project_summary: A three-layer summary: (1) the current loop (in progress, the top ready issues, requirements whose children are all finished) (2) waiting on a human (In Review and how long it has waited; over 48 hours is marked) (3) input from outside (unanswered feedback). Use it when you start work
server.mcp.tool.ready_issues: Issues that can be started (open, not In Progress, and every blocked_by resolved)
server.mcp.tool.report_verify: Records the results of verification commands run in a local shell (a comment and a verify record, marked as self-reported via MCP). The server does not run the commands. First get the list and body_sha256 with verify_issue, run every command in the list in the same order, then send. It is rejected with body_changed if the body has changed, and rejected if the commands differ from the list. If the CLI (looptrack issue verify <ID>) is available, use it instead (the code runs and measures the commands, and no mark is added)
server.mcp.tool.set_status: Change the status (comment leaves a comment at the same time; a per-project rule may reject the change)
server.mcp.tool.setup: Returns how far issue tracking (hooks, the CLI, the guide text) is installed in this AI's working environment, and the steps. It returns the install command, the SHA-256 of the files to install and the download URLs for the kind of AI that connected (clientInfo). Call it once at the start of your work. Pass the absolute path of the git root of the working directory in the workspace argument (the judgment is whether that working directory is installed). When a choice is needed on whether to install the loop engineering set (loop), the first call returns only the question and no command. Show the question to the user as it is, get their answer, then call again with the user's answer in the loop argument (yes / no) (and the same workspace), and exactly one install command matching the answer comes back. The AI never decides the answer and adds loop by itself
server.mcp.tool.update_issue: Update the body (the full text in markdown) or fields. It fails when version differs from the current one; start again from get_issue
server.mcp.tool.usage_missing: AI change operations with no token usage attached, and the coverage (operations a person typed at a terminal are out of scope). To fill them in, run looptrack issue usage attach <ID> for each issue
server.mcp.tool.usage_report: Totals of token usage for a report (a given period, or since the last report): total, by issue, by case (group=label), by label, by type, by stage, by AI, by conversation, and unattributed. Conversations excluded from reports are shown separately. Register the report you made in the ledger with add_usage_ledger
server.mcp.tool.verify_issue: Returns an issue's verification commands (the "## Verify commands" section of the body) and the latest verify record. This tool neither runs nor records the commands. To run and record them, use looptrack issue verify <ID> in a local shell (if the CLI is not available, run them locally and send the results with report_verify)

worktree.usage:
Usage: looptrack worktree <subcommand> ...

Tidy up git worktrees and branches whose work is finished. **Nothing is deleted by default.**

  list                  List the worktrees and branches (what can go, why the rest is kept, when each was last active)
  prune [--yes]         Clean up. Without --yes it only shows what would be deleted
  mark [--session <ID>] [--yes] Record that this session is using this worktree (never written for the main worktree; a different session's marker is kept unless --yes is passed)

Common options:
  --dir <path>      Anywhere inside the repository (defaults to the working directory)
  --base <branch>   Merge target (defaults to main, or master if there is no main)
  --min-age <time>  Keep worktrees newer than this (default 30m, so a worktree another session is still using is left alone)

A worktree is deleted only when **all** of these hold: it is not the main one, it is merged, it has no uncommitted
changes, it is not locked, its branch is not published to the remote, and it has been idle for at least --min-age.
Anything that misses one of them is kept, with the reason shown.

A worktree whose branch tracks a remote (and whose upstream still exists) is treated as a permanent one shared by the
repository and is never cleaned up (worktrees used for deployment or for switching, for example). Once the upstream is
gone, the branch is treated as an ordinary temporary one.
